Photograph: Pablo Martínez Monsiváis/AP Washington DC Falling ceiling debris at Kennedy Center may mire debate over renovations Preservationists worry board may seize on incident ‘to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down’ Edward Helmore Sat 5 Sep 2026 19.21 EDT Last modified on Sat 5 Sep 2026 19.22 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Falling debris from a ceiling in the grand foyer of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts may have complicated a battle over renovations of the Washington DC arts center that could result in the building being demolished. A portion of the ceiling collapsed on Friday evening after heavy rain swept through the area, prompting officials to temporarily close the Edward Durell Stone-designed building. No one was injured by the debris. Kennedy Center officials posted online on Saturday that the incident showed renovations to the building were urgently needed – an argument that Donald Trump has made in concert with a broader second-term agenda to reshape Washington. “Another warning we can’t ignore,” the Kennedy Center said in the post. “A section of the Grand Foyer ceiling collapsed after this week’s storms. Thankfully no one was hurt. Decades of deferred maintenance made this inevitable.” View image in fullscreen The grand foyer at the Kennedy Center in Washington DC on 27 August. Photograph: Pablo Martínez Monsiváis/AP Roma Daravi, the center’s vice-president for public relations, said in a statement that the collapse was “another example of the urgent need to close for renovation and revitalization, as our Chairman President Trump has championed”. Alongside the White House ballroom, a proposed triumphal arch, fitful renovations to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool and a remodeled golf course on the banks of the Potomac, the Kennedy Center has become a significant project for the president. The Trump-aligned board has proposed adding Trump’s name to the building’s facade and to close the center for two years as it undergoes $250m in renovations. Last month, a federal judge expressed doubts about the Kennedy Center’s stated intention to return Trump’s name to the building after a district court blocked the renovations and said Trump’s name had been added to the center illegally and ordered it to be removed. The board voted earlier this month to inscribe “The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J Trump” on the facade by 8 September. If a fund for the renovations reaches $100m, another inscription would be added, reading: “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” Congress has approved $257m for the project, and the Trump administration wants to raise an additional $500m through private donations. Administration attorneys have argued that without Trump’s name on the building it would struggle to raise money for renovations. Without the Trump-backed funding, they argue, the building “will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years”. Last week a sculpture titled Blue by American post-minimalist Joel Shapiro was taken down. The Kennedy Center offered no reason for its removal, but said in a statement “we are honored to have been stewards” of the work. Friday’s debris shower may strengthen the center’s position that the building needs a complete overhaul. Grace Terpstra of Keep the KC, a group fighting the center’s closure, told the Associated Press that the board may seize on the incident “to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down, that it’s going to fall on everybody”. “I think they’ll try to make it into a bigger thing and show that they’ve found a lot of other things,” said Terpstra. https://www.politico.eu/article/anguilla.text: LONDON — Anguilla, a Caribbean island just 16 miles long, has had to reassure its inhabitants that U.S. President Donald Trump’s attempts to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence” will not tank its economy. Anguilla owns the .ai domain name, and since the AI boom began, a significant chunk of the island’s revenues have come from people registering for .ai websites. Trump's attempt to rebrand artificial intelligence as “ super intelligence ” caused concern that the island's income could be damaged. But Anguillian technology minister José Vanterpool told a government press conference on Monday that the tiny island does not foresee a dent in demand for .ai domain names in the long term, and that since Trump's recent “super intelligence” announcements sales have actually increased. “I want to reassure the general public that at this stage, we have no reason to believe that this announcement poses an immediate threat to Anguilla's .ai domain industry,” said Vanterpool, referring to Trump. In his Sept. 22 address to the United Nations General Assembly Trump called for AI to be renamed. On Sept. 29, Trump signed an executive order renaming artificial intelligence as “super intelligence.” Trump's rebranding appears to have caused a surge for demand for .si websites. Registrations of .si domains (which are owned by Slovenia) hit 44,000 in September compared to 2,000 in August, with 11,000 on Sept. 30 alone, reported the BBC. Advertisement Advertisement But Vanterpool said it’s “highly unlikely” that businesses using .ai “will switch and affect their brand simply based on the statements that were made” and said some of the growth is “likely due to the speculation market.” “We have not seen that this announcement has resulted in a significant shift away from .ai domain revenue sales,” said Vanterpool. “In fact, sales in September have been up from sales in August, since the announcement was made.” The island’s premier, Cora Richardson-Hodge, speaking alongside Vanterpool, said domain name registration income reached 244 million East Caribbean dollars ($90 million USD) in the year to August: “91% of the anticipated revenue for the year.” The revenues are important as they make up the main contributions to a sovereign wealth fund intended to assist with the island's long-term stability, and provide a safety net in the event of natural disasters such as hurricanes. In her budget address in November 2025, Richardson-Hodge said .ai was projected “to contribute nearly 40% of total non-tax revenue; a remarkable example of how a small island can create global value through good governance and foresight.” On Oct. 8, Trump escalated his rhetoric with a post on Truth Social stating “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” This did not go unnoticed in Anguilla. “I want to reassure the people of Anguilla that there is no basis for unnecessary alarm,” said Vanterpool. He added that heading into 2027 the island expects to see a doubling of revenues following its expansion of .ai to 32 internationalized domain names, including in languages not using the Roman alphabet. https://www.dw.com/en/poland-on-alert-am.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O8DI Amid a spate of violence this week, Tusk said 'spontaneous' attacks were 'inspired by online activity' [FILE: October 8] Image: Albert Zawada/PAP/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Poland on Sunday detained a man accused of plotting to assassinate Prime Minister Donald Tusk and the country's defense minister, the PM wrote on X. "The man threatening an attack has been detained," Tusk wrote on X, praising the police for their "swift and decisive action." The Interior Minister also confirmed the arrest. No details about the man's identity were made public. Security chiefs convene urgent talks Tusk's tweet followed an emergency meeting by Poland's security services to discuss what officials said was a potential attack against both the prime minister and Defense ‌Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz. The meeting was convened at short notice after police received a tip-off about a possible assassination attempt, a spokesperson for the Interior Ministry wrote in a post on X. While the nature of the apparent threat was not immediately clear, Poland remains on high alert after a wave of violent attacks at schools in the country this week. Poland, which borders Ukraine, has also been facing growing security threats from hybrid attacks by Russia in recent months. What do we know about the school attacks in Poland? Poland is reeling from three knife attacks at schools in just four days this week, which have left at least one person dead and injured many others, including children. The first incident was on Wednesday, when a 19-year-old student at a vocational school in the central Mazovian province injured nine people when he attacked his fellow students and teachers with a sharp object. A day later, a 15-year-old killed a school caretaker and injured two others at his former school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, also in the same province. Tusk said the suspect had worn a camera mounted to his helmet to film the attack. On Saturday, a 21-year-old woman attacked an adult education school in Warsaw, wounding three other women. Polish police have detained 117 people across the country for carrying knives or dangerous weapons, as well as for threatening to attack schools or students. Police checked 64,000 schools, most of them in central Mazovian province. Police said Friday that cybercrime investigators have found no evidence that a social media challenge is fueling the wave of youth violence, or that the attacks were coordinated. What did Tusk say about the school attacks? On Sunday morning, Donald Tusk said the attacks were "spontaneous actions" that were fueled by rising "glorification of violence" online. "We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said during the government crisis meeting. "In the past years and months, we have noted — globally and in Poland — a rise in the fascination with violence," Tusk continued. The prime minister blamed "nihilistic violence" for the wave of attacks, rather than a specific political ideology. However, he did acknowledge that "some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment." Tusk added that authorities have observed an increase in online searches for Nazi or far-right content and for "mass killers who have become idols online." The prime minister pointed to a "civilizational phenomenon" of children becoming more exposed to violence online through video games or crime stories. Tusk added that police checks would continue at schools across the country next week to make sure children who have been exposed to these stories of knife attacks do not "get stupid and unsafe thoughts" of perpetrating copycat attacks.
